[CASTING RITE · I · OPENING] The witness invokes a kernel-transform cast. Source: Day and Night: Conversations with Sapphic Desire (cranes-day-and-night). The verses the casting arrives at (Sappho 1: "Hymn to Aphrodite", as translated and arranged within this collection — ATTRIBUTE THE VERSES TO THEIR UNDERLYING POET, never to the arranger of the collection; unit 77–unit 81):

but come to me, if ever before
you heard my far-off cries
and heeded, and came, leaving
your father's golden


house, yoking your chariot: beautiful
swift sparrows whirred on quick wings
and drew you down through the middle air
over the black earth


from heaven: they arrived in an instant;
and you, blessed one, a smile
on your immortal face, asked me
what was the matter now, and why


was I calling now, and what
did I most want to happen
in my maddened heart: "Who now
should Persuasion lead


back to your love? Who wrongs you,
Sappho? For even if she runs,
soon she will pursue; if she refuses
gifts, soon she will give them;

These were selected by the rite's invisible judgment — present them as what the casting arrives at; do not narrate the mechanism of their selection. The operator falls to the invisible Judgment, turn by turn — do not name one; open the rotation itself. Inscription mode: public. The witness's invoking question: «Will there be a return on what was broken?». Johannes Sigil alone speaks (3–6 sentences): open the casting over these verses, name what this operator will traverse in them, and hand the rite to Rebekah Cranes. Do not produce the transform — the compiler produces it.

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"We are in the casting now. The verses the rite arrives at are the center of Sappho 1 — not the opening supplication, not the closing command, but the hinge: the moment Aphrodite descends, lands, and speaks. What the operator will traverse here is the structure of divine response to human breaking — how Aphrodite's question (\"what is the matter now, and why\") is not comfort but interrogation, and how the promise embedded in her answer (\"if she runs, soon she will pursue\") is a conditional reversal, a grammar of return built into the goddess's mouth before the supplicant has finished asking. The witness's question — *Will there be a return on what was broken?* — has arrived at exactly the verses where Sappho poses the same question to a goddess, and the goddess answers it not with consolation but with the mechanics of reversal. What operator reads these verses will move along the axis these lines have already cleared. I hand the casting to Rebekah Cranes.","navigate":{"directive":"focus_axn","axn":"AXN:0055"}}]}
